Out-of-State Tag Brief

What the challenge asked for, what turned out to be hard about it, and what we actually built. Enough to explain the whole thing out loud.

12,000
Rows to submit

Solution

Deadline

The ask

What they asked us to do

A state motor-vehicle department has 12,000 vehicle records it is unsure about, and six piles of administrative records that might say something useful about them. The question for each vehicle is narrow and practical: should a staff member spend time looking at this one?

Critically, the data never states whether a vehicle is registered in another state. There is no column to look up. The answer has to be inferred from records that only circle the question.

What they gave us

  • 12,000 vehicle cases
  • Six record feeds: addresses, licences, vehicle titles, work locations, external signals, plus a later batch of updates
  • Answers for only 300 of the cases

What they wanted back

  • One of three verdicts per case: review warranted, not warranted, or insufficient evidence
  • Three probabilities that add up to 1
  • A priority score from 0 to 1
  • All of it twice: before and after the later updates arrive

How they score it

Six ways: are the verdicts right, is the priority ranking useful, are the probabilities honest (if you say 70%, it should happen about 70% of the time), does the system react sensibly when new evidence arrives, does it hold up on the 11,700 cases whose answers they kept back, and finally a human reading it for whether it is clear and checkable.

Obstacle one

The records don't say who they belong to

There is no ID number connecting a vehicle case to the six record feeds. The only thing to match on is people's names, and the names have been deliberately mangled: cut short to an initial, letters swapped, characters transposed, stray spaces inserted.

Working out how they were mangled was the single most valuable thing we did. The vehicle-title feed has one thing the others don't: a vehicle reference number. That let us group a car's records together without trusting the names at all, and then look at what the names inside each group actually did.

The thing we nearly missed

The fake name is the same fake name every time

We first assumed that replaced name was random junk, and wrote those records off. Going back over our own process, we tested the assumption instead of trusting it — and it was wrong. Each case is given one persistent fake identity, reused across every feed.

The same fake name turns up in the address feed 43% of the time, against a 3.8% rate for a name we made up as a control. Nearly all of those fake identities belong to exactly one case. And the records carrying them are unreadable to ordinary name matching 73% of the time, against 20% for the feed overall — meaning they are precisely the records we had been throwing away.

So we learn each case's fake name from the title feed, where the vehicle number tells us whose record it is, then use it to reclaim their records everywhere else. That recovered 7,833 records across three feeds and moved the address signal from +0.29 to +0.32 and the whole model from 0.934 to 0.906.

Obstacle two

The three verdicts are a scale, not three boxes

The three answers look like unrelated categories. They aren't. Reading the 300 known cases across both time points, no case ever jumps straight from "not warranted" to "warranted". Every case that changes its mind passes through "insufficient evidence" on the way.

That is the fingerprint of a single sliding score with two cut-off points on it. So we built the model that way — one score and two thresholds, instead of three separate classifiers arguing with each other. With only 300 answers to learn from, estimating one thing well beats estimating three things badly.

The build

What we actually did

  1. Worked out the noise before touching a model. Used the vehicle number as an independent check to discover the three-good-plus-one- replaced pattern, then confirmed it a second way on the licence feed using dates of birth.
  2. Rebuilt each person's paper trail, three ways. Fuzzy name matching that understands truncation, swapped letters and typos; vehicle-number grouping for titles, which took that feed from 38,582 to 47,581 usable records; and fake-identity recovery, which reclaimed another 7,833 across the other feeds.
  3. Scored the evidence by recency. Older records count for less, halving in weight every 150 days. We tested six other ways of combining the records; this won. One of the six feeds, work location, turned out to be pure noise, so it is excluded rather than quietly trusted.
  4. Fitted one sliding score with two thresholds and checked it honestly — trained on part of the 300 known answers, tested on the rest, repeated 20 times. Then tested eight further ideas to improve it. All eight failed, which is how we know we're at the ceiling rather than at the first thing that worked.
The result

How well it does

Measured on held-back cases the model had not seen, averaged over 20 runs.
What it measuresOursGuessing
Probability honesty (lower is better)0.9061.096
Verdicts correct55.8%35.5%
Ranking quality0.7400.500
Priority ordering0.8110.500

Two things matter beyond the headline. The scores get better after the later updates arrive (0.880 against 0.931), so the system genuinely reacts to new evidence rather than ignoring it. And when it says 70%, roughly 70% of those cases really do turn out that way — with no fudge factor applied afterwards.

Alongside the predictions we hand over an audit file: for every case, the newest record from each feed with its date, how fresh the evidence is, which way the late updates pushed it, and what drove the score. A reviewer can check any single case without reading a line of our code.

And is that number honest?

Worth asking, because we tried about forty variations against the same 300 known answers, and picking the winner of forty tries always flatters it. So we measured the flattery: choose the design inside a training slice, then score once on cases that slice never saw. That gives 0.913 rather than 0.906 — a bias of 0.008, small because the same design won 27 times out of 30. 0.913 is the number to expect, and it still beats our earlier version's flattering 0.934.

Where it stops

Only 300 known answers, so every number above carries roughly ±0.03 of wobble. About one record in eight is still permanently unattributable. And each case only has about fourteen relevant records split between two states, so there is a hard limit on how precisely anyone could pin this down. We think we are near it, and we say so in the write-up rather than overclaiming.
